paragraphs.original: This work investigates how an object detector small enough for embedded hardware can be trained when real training images are scarce, using wildlife species recognition as the test case. The deployment context is a consumer binocular that classifies the mammal a user is looking at, on the device itself, and without a network connection. That fixes two hard constraints: a per-frame latency budget on a mobile system-on-chip, and a class universe of $225$ mammal species rather than the few dozen coarse classes of a general detection benchmark. The detector has to locate the animal and classify its species, and classification carries the difficulty, since many of these species differ only in fine markings (\Cref{sec:results_granularity_gaps}). Two training strategies are compared: distilling a much larger fine-tuned teacher model into a small student model and fine-tuning that same student directly on the wildlife dataset. Of the $225$ classes, $50$ retain fewer than $150$ usable real photographs each, so this work also asks whether diffusion-generated imagery can provide the missing real data, and how far a detector trained on it still transfers to real photographs.

paragraphs.original: Species identification in the field has begun to move from printed field guides into the optics themselves. The \textit{AX Visio} binocular \cite{AXVisio} runs a species-recognition model on board and classifies the animal the user is already looking at. The classification must happen while the animal is still within the field of view. This rules out sending the frame to a remote service. The habitats in which the device is used also rule this out, since network coverage cannot be assumed there. The recognition model therefore has to fit a mobile system-on-chip and meet a per-frame latency budget on it. The deployment target is the \textit{Qualcomm QCS605} \cite{QCS605}, a mobile platform combining a \textit{Hexagon 685} digital signal processor with an \textit{Adreno 615} graphics processor, whose compute budget excludes the model scales at which detection accuracy is normally reported. Development and benchmarking in this work targeted a \textit{Raspberry Pi 400} \cite{ltdBuyRaspberryPi} instead, for the software-maturity reasons set out in \Cref{sec:results_embedded_benchmark}.

paragraphs.original: Accurate detection comes at the cost of model size and inference speed. The most accurate models are large \cite{zouObjectDetection202023}, which makes an embedded target difficult to achieve. The teacher model used in this study has approximately $193\,\mathrm{M}$ parameters, compared to $2.71\,\mathrm{M}$ for the student model that was actually exported to the device. Knowledge distillation is the established solution to such a discrepancy. Early work on model compression trained a small, fast model to reproduce the outputs of a large ensemble \cite{buciluaModelCompression2006}. Later work generalized the idea by having the student match the teacher's softened output distribution rather than its hard predictions \cite{hintonDistillingKnowledgeNeural2015}. Whether that mechanism survives a move from general object classes to fine-grained species is the question this work was built around.

paragraphs.original: Two properties of the wildlife domain make that question non-trivial. The class universe is fine-grained: many of the $225$ classes differ only in fine markings, and a detector has to learn exactly those markings \cite{weiFineGrainedImageAnalysis2022}. The available imagery is long-tailed, with a few well-photographed species dominating the corpus while most are supported by comparatively few usable photographs \cite{zhangDeepLongTailedLearning2023}. Machine-learning work on wildlife imagery treats both properties as recurring obstacles rather than as edge cases \cite{tuiaPerspectivesMachineLearning2022}. Camera-trap detection is also known to degrade sharply once a model is evaluated at locations it was not trained on \cite{beeryRecognitionTerraIncognita2018}, so a thin per-class image pool is a generalization problem and not only a sample-count problem.

paragraphs.original: Text-to-image diffusion models \cite{rombachHighResolutionImageSynthesis2022} offer the one intervention that can add appearance content a data-poor class's own photographs do not contain, such as an unrecorded pose, habitat or lighting condition. Training a classifier from scratch on generated images, however, required roughly five times as many of them to match real images of the same classes \cite{heSyntheticDataGenerative2023}, and prompting an off-the-shelf generator with bare class names produced a very poor classifier \cite{aziziSyntheticDataDiffusion2023}. Earlier work by the present author found that generated image context conferred no downstream detection advantage over per-pixel random noise on a small-object car-detection task \cite{hedrichGeneratingSyntheticDatasets2026}, which is what leaves the choice of generator an open question here (\Cref{sec:generator_comparison}). Synthetic imagery is therefore treated in this work as a supplement whose usefulness is measured rather than assumed.

paragraphs.original: Wildlife species recognition for a handheld optic exercises both problems at once, which makes it a demanding test case. It combines a fixed latency ceiling, a fine-grained class universe, a long-tailed image supply, and a product requirement that the resulting weights remain commercially licensable. None of these constraints was constructed for the experiment.

paragraphs.original: The objective is to build, train and evaluate a nano-scale detector for wildlife species recognition on embedded hardware, and to measure which of the available training strategies actually helps it. Nano-scale here means the smallest variants of a detector family, at roughly one to three million parameters. Detection accuracy means mean average precision over the species classes, which scores the box and the species together, so a correctly located animal with the wrong species name counts as a miss. It is reported throughout on the mixed test set, the union of the real and synthetic held-out images, with the real test set breakout stated alongside it every time (\Cref{sec:mixed_default}). paragraphs.original: \item Does knowledge distillation from a fine-tuned teacher model into a nano-scale student model yield higher detection accuracy than fine-tuning the same student directly on the wildlife dataset, given the domain shift from COCO-style classes to $225$ mammal species?

\item Which synthetic-image generator produces the most useful training data for this domain, and do the two criteria available before any detector is trained, apparent visual realism and per-image price, predict that ranking?

\item How does the composition of a class's training data, from synthetic images alone through a large pool of real photographs, affect detection accuracy, and does accuracy measured on the mixed test set hold up on the real test set alone?
\item Does a nano-scale detector meet the per-frame latency budget of the target hardware without quantization or any other compression step, measured on a target-adjacent proxy device?

The four questions did not receive equal effort. Roughly $80\%$ of the available time went into dataset construction and synthetic-image generation, so questions $2$ and $3$ carry the bulk of the experimental work. Question $1$ is answered from a single teacher and student pairing at one distillation hyperparameter setting, and question $4$ from a single full-precision runtime measurement on the proxy device. \Cref{sec:limitations} treats that reduced scope as a named limitation. Each question is restated and answered in turn in \Cref{chapter:discussion_conclusion}, from the evidence assembled in \Cref{chapter:results}.

paragraphs.original: The remainder of this thesis is organized into four chapters and an appendix. The \hyperref[chapter:literature_review]{\textit{Literature Review}} traces object detection from its two architectural lineages to the nano-scale variants relevant here, then covers generative image models, the sim-to-real gap, synthetic-image quality evaluation and the long-tail literature, and closes with knowledge distillation, embedded inference feasibility and the evaluation literature this work's metrics draw on. \hyperref[chapter:methods_implementation]{\textit{Methods and Implementation}} describes how the dataset and the experiments were built, from class taxonomy and image sourcing through curation, synthetic supplementation and augmentation, then a sub-study comparing ten generators across three prompt regimes, and finally the training setup and the evaluation framework.

paragraphs.original: The \hyperref[chapter:results]{\textit{Results}} chapter reports the generator comparison, detection performance across the training bands and test domains, the distillation-versus-direct-fine-tuning comparison, and the runtime benchmark on the proxy device. \hyperref[chapter:discussion_conclusion]{\textit{Discussion and Conclusion}} answers the four research questions from that evidence, states the limitations, and proposes the further work they motivate.
